title-group.article-title: Thermo-Kinetic Analysis of Corncob-Water Hyacinth Co-Pyrolysis for Synergistic Insights and Biochar Characteristics for Soil Amendment

abstract.p: The co-pyrolysis of corncob (CC) and water hyacinth (WH) was investigated to characterize their thermal decomposition behavior, kinetic properties, and resulting biochars. Thermogravimetric (TGA) and derivative thermogravimetric (DTG) analyses were conducted at heating rates of 5 and 20 °C min−1 for the individual feedstocks and their blends. Biochars from CC, WH, and CC50:WH50 were produced at 350 °C and characterized for physicochemical properties. At 5 °C min−1, apparent activation energies estimated using the Coats–Redfern method were 135.4, 73.2, 83.1, 96.4, and 103.6 kJ mol−1 for CC, WH, CC30:WH70, CC50:WH50, respectively. Experimental and theoretical thermogravimetric profiles were compared to assess deviations from additive behavior. Biochar yields ranged from 39.22% to 46.17%, while mean pH values ranged from 9.34 to 9.56. One-way analysis of variance indicated significant treatment differences in yield, electrical conductivity, total nitrogen, available phosphorus, cation exchange capacity, and bulk density, whereas pH differences were not significant. WH biochar exhibited the highest electrical conductivity, total nitrogen, and available phosphorus, while CC50:WH50 had the highest cation exchange capacity and bulk density. These findings show that feedstock composition influences thermal behavior and biochar properties.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Renewable wastes, including agricultural residues, animal wastes, and bioprocessing wastes, are increasingly considered valuable biomass resources because of their carbon content and availability [1]. One important product obtained from biomass conversion is biochar. Biochar is a carbon-rich material that can be used for improving soil fertility and productivity, carbon storage, and the retention of dissolved pollutants in soil [2]. It is produced in inert atmospheres and at comparatively modest carbonization temperatures [1]. In recent years, increasing attention has been given to converting bio-waste into biochar due to its potential environmental, economic, and sustainability benefits, as well as growing interest in its applications in energy and environmental management [1,3]. Biochar derived from biomass, including invasive plant residues, contains several essential nutrients and mineral elements that can contribute to soil fertility [2,4]. Its carbonaceous structure and nutrient content may also influence soil physical properties such as water retention, aeration, and aggregation, thereby providing conditions that can support plant growth [2].

Water hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes) (WH) is widely recognized as a highly invasive aquatic weed [5]. In Ethiopia, its expansion in lakes has created challenges for several activities, including transportation, hydropower generation, agriculture, aquaculture, and tourism [6]. Considerable quantities of the biomass are removed manually and mechanically to control infestation, but the collected material is often disposed of without adequate conversion into useful products. For example, approximately 1,990,787.80 tons of water hyacinth biomass and 554,523.80 tons of dry biomass have been estimated to be available annually from Lake Tana [7]. Converting this biomass into biochar could provide an alternative approach for utilizing the accumulated weed while generating a product with potential soil-amendment applications [4].

Although water hyacinth has a relatively low biochar yield due to its low lignin content, its biochar can retain mineral nutrients and provide beneficial physicochemical properties for potential soil-amendment applications [8]. Co-pyrolysis involves the simultaneous thermochemical conversion of two or more feedstocks under the same operating conditions. Combining different biomass feedstocks can alter their thermal degradation behavior and the properties of the resulting products because of interactions between their components [9,10]. Therefore, the effects of blending should be determined from the observed thermal behavior rather than assuming that co-pyrolysis will always result in a positive synergistic effect.

Soil acidity is another important consideration in Ethiopia, where approximately 43% of agricultural land has been reported to be affected by soil acidity [11]. Agricultural residues such as straw, cobs, husks, and stalks are abundant lignocellulosic resources that can be considered for thermochemical conversion [1]. Corncob (CC) is a readily available but comparatively underutilized agricultural residue in Ethiopia. Previous research has estimated that maize-producing districts generate substantial quantities of maize residues, including leaves, cobs, and stalks [12]. Corncob contains cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, whose proportions influence its thermal decomposition behavior and the characteristics of the resulting biochar. Consequently, CC can serve as a suitable feedstock for biochar production through pyrolysis and may provide a useful biomass resource for soil-amendment and energy-related applications [1,13].

Understanding biomass decomposition helps select suitable pyrolysis conditions and improve thermochemical conversion processes. Kinetic approaches such as the Coats–Redfern method have been applied to evaluate the thermal degradation of various agro-industrial residues [14]. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) is also widely used to investigate biomass thermal degradation and estimate associated kinetic parameters [15,16]. However, the thermo-kinetic behavior of CC and WH during co-pyrolysis, particularly how their blending ratio affects thermal decomposition and the characteristics of the resulting biochar, remains insufficiently investigated. Comparative TG/DTG and kinetic analyses of the individual feedstocks and their blends can therefore provide information on their decomposition behavior and possible interactions during co-pyrolysis.

Therefore, this study investigates the co-pyrolysis of water hyacinth (WH) and corncob (CC) for biochar production. The thermal decomposition behavior and kinetic parameters of CC, WH, and their blends were evaluated using TG/DTG analysis at different heating rates. Experimental and theoretical mass-loss behaviors were compared to assess deviations from additive decomposition and identify composition-dependent thermal interactions. Biochars produced from CC, WH, and their CC50:WH50 blend were further characterized for selected physical and chemical properties relevant to their potential use as soil amendments.

sec.title: 2. Materials and Methods
sec.p: Corncob (CC) and water hyacinth (WH) were collected from agricultural fields in the Jimma area and from locations surrounding Lake Koka, Ethiopia, respectively. The collected feedstocks were pulverized and oven-dried at 110 °C for 24 h. After drying, the materials were ground and sieved to obtain a relatively uniform particle size as seen in Figure 1. The feedstocks were subsequently mixed on a mass basis at CC: WH ratios of 30:70, 50:50, and 70:30, in addition to the unblended CC (100:0) and WH (0:100) samples as shown in Table 1.

sec.title: 2.1. Biomass Characterization
sec.p: Using gravimetric techniques, a proximate analysis of CC and WH was conducted to ascertain their moisture, volatile matter, ash, and fixed-carbon contents [17]. The difference was used to determine the fixed-carbon fraction. Table 2 summarizes the ultimate-analysis data for the two feedstocks, which were obtained from previously published sources, along with the relevant references.

sec.title: 2.2. Procedure for Thermogravimetric Experiments
sec.p: Thermogravimetric measurements were conducted on CC, WH, and their blends to assess their thermal decomposition characteristics. For each test, approximately 8.7 mg of sample was placed in the DTG-60H thermal analyzer (Shimadzu Corporation, Japan) and heated from 22 to 800 °C at 5 and 20 °C/min under a nitrogen flow rate of 50 mL/min. The TG profiles were used to monitor changes in sample mass with increasing temperature, while the corresponding DTG curves were generated from the derivative of mass with respect to temperature. The resulting mass-loss profiles were examined according to the principal stages of biomass thermal decomposition [15].(1)(dWdt)=−1Wo(dmdt) where Wo denotes the initial mass of the sample.

sec.title: 2.3. Kinetic Modeling of Biomass
sec.p: The thermal decomposition kinetics of CC, WH, and their blends were analyzed using the Coats–Redfern integral model-fitting approach. The conversion fraction (α\alpha) was obtained from the initial, instantaneous, and final sample masses, and the apparent activation energy (Ea) and pre-exponential factor (A) were estimated from the linearized kinetic expression. The applicability of different solid-state reaction models was subsequently examined using the Criado master-plot method [20].

For a heterogeneous solid-state reaction, the conversion rate can be expressed in general form as(2)(dαdt)=k(T)f(α) where the temperature dependence is represented by the Arrhenius relationship:(3)(dαdt)=Aexp(−ERT)f(α)

Here, f(α)f(\alpha) represents the differential reaction model, A is the pre-exponential factor, Ea is the apparent activation energy, R is the universal gas constant, and T is the absolute temperature.

The extent of conversion was calculated from the change in sample mass according to(4)a=W0−WtW0−Wf where W0, wt, and wf denote the initial sample mass, the mass at temperature T, and the final mass, respectively, and(5)β=dTdt where β\beta is the heating rate (°C/min), T is the absolute temperature (K), and t is time. Coats–Redfern

The Coats–Redfern procedure was applied to obtain the kinetic parameters by approximating the temperature integral in the non-isothermal reaction equation. For a constant heating rate and a selected reaction model g(α)g(\alpha), the linearized form is given by [18](6)ln[g(α)T^2]=ln[AoRβEa]−ERT

A plot of ln[(g(α))/T2] against 1/T was used to determine the kinetic parameters. The slope of the fitted line corresponds to -Ea/R, whereas the intercept provides the basis for calculating the pre-exponential factor Ao [18]. To identify the reaction mechanism that best describes the thermal conversion, the experimental reduced rate was compared with theoretical master curves using the Criado approach [20]. The corresponding reduced-rate expression is(7)Z(α)Z(0.5)=f(α)g(α)f(0.5)g(0.5)=(TαT0.5)(dαdt)α(dαdt)0.5 where the concentration-dependent terms f(α) and g(α) are shown in Table 3, respectively. Tα represents the temperature at conversion α; T0.5: Temperature at conversion (α) = 0.5; (dα/dt) α: Conversion varies with time at conversion (α); and (dα/dt)0.5: Conversion varies with time at conversion (α) = 0.5. The right-side equation displays the reduced rate, which was determined using experimental data [19]. In contrast, the left side shows a theoretical master plot depicting each distinctive reaction mechanism, denoted by the formula [f(α)g(α)/f (0.5) g (0.5)].

sec.title: 2.4. Evaluation of Synergistic Interactions Between WH and CC
sec.p: Synergistic interactions between water hyacinth (WH) and corncob (CC) were evaluated by comparing the experimentally observed thermal behavior of the blends with the theoretical additive behavior expected from the individual feedstocks. The theoretical value of each parameter was calculated using the following equations:(8)Wtheoretical=XWHWWH+XCCWCC(9)ΔW=WExperimental−WTheoretical where W stands for mass loss, activation energy, component content, etc., and XWH and XCC are the ratios of CC and WH in the blends, respectively. The values of ΔW were used to examine the co-pyrolysis’s antagonistic or synergistic effects [22]. A negative ΔW value indicates a positive synergistic effect and an accelerated co-pyrolysis process, whereas a positive ΔW value suggests a passive synergistic effect.

sec.title: 2.5. Production and Characterization of Biochar Samples
sec.p: Biochar was produced from corncob (CC), water hyacinth (WH), and their CC50:WH50 blend using a fixed-bed reactor at 350 °C. For each treatment, a 6 kg dry feedstock sample was heated at 2 °C/min under oxygen-limited conditions for 120 min, as shown in Table 4. The reactor was equipped with a temperature-control system, a gear motor-driven stirrer, a condensation system, and a K-type thermocouple for temperature monitoring, as illustrated in Figure 2. Following pyrolysis, the reactor was allowed to cool to room temperature. The produced biochar was weighed, milled, and sieved to obtain particles smaller than 2 mm before physicochemical characterization. Three independent pyrolysis batches were conducted for each treatment. Biochar yield was calculated separately for each batch, and the results were expressed as the mean ± standard deviation (SD).

sec.title: 2.6. Procedures for Determining Physicochemical Properties
sec.p: The Nekemte Soil Research Center Laboratory, Oromia Agricultural Research Institute (OARI), determined the physicochemical properties of the produced biochar samples. The analyses included biochar yield, bulk density, pH, electrical conductivity (EC), cation exchange capacity (CEC), total nitrogen (TN), and available phosphorus (P).

sec.title: 2.6.1. Biochar Yield and Bulk Density
sec.p: Biochar yield was determined from the mass of biochar produced after pyrolysis relative to the initial dry mass of feedstock. The yield was calculated as(10)Yield(%)=WbiocharWbiomass∗100 where Wbiomass is the weight of sun-dried biomass (kg) and Wbiochar is the weight of biochar (kg).

The bulk density of the biochar samples was determined from the mass of a known volume of biochar and calculated as(11)Bulkdensity=WdVd where Wd is the biochar’s weight (g) and Vd, is its volume (cm3).

sec.title: 2.6.2. The pH and Electrical Conductivity (EC)
sec.p: The pH and EC of the biochar samples were determined using a 1:10 biochar-to-deionized-water suspension. Briefly, 5 g of biochar was mixed with 50 mL of deionized water and stirred for 1 h. The suspension was allowed to settle for approximately 30 min before measuring pH and EC using calibrated meters [23,24].

sec.title: 2.6.3. Determination of Cation Exchange Capacity
sec.p: The cation exchange capacity (CEC) of the biochar samples was measured by ammonium acetate saturation, following the procedure described in [25]. Briefly, 1.0 ± 0.05 g of biochar was equilibrated with 40 mL of 1 M ammonium acetate (pH 7.0) for 15 h. After filtration, the samples were washed with neutral 1 M ammonium acetate and ethanol, and the adsorbed NH4+ was displaced with 90 mL of 2 M KCl. The NH4+ concentration in the extract was measured using a FIAlab 2500 flow-injection autoanalyzer (FIAlab Instruments, Inc., Seattle, WA, USA), and CEC was calculated from the amount of displaced NH4+ per unit mass of biochar [25].

sec.title: 2.6.4. Determination of Total Nitrogen (TN)
sec.p: The total nitrogen content of the biochar samples was determined using the Kjeldahl method. The method involves acid digestion of the sample to convert organic nitrogen into ammonium, followed by determination of the resulting ammonium nitrogen. The TN content was expressed as a percentage of the dry sample weight [26].

sec.title: 2.6.5. Available Nutrients
sec.p: Available phosphorus (P) was extracted using 2% formic acid following Wang et al. [27]. Briefly, 0.35 g of biochar was mixed with 35 mL of 2% formic acid and shaken at 160 rpm for 30 min. The suspension was centrifuged for 10 min, and the supernatant was filtered through Whatman No. 41 filter paper. Phosphorus concentration was determined using a FIAlab 2500 flow-injection autoanalyzer (FIAlab Instruments, Inc., USA) [27].

sec.title: 2.6.6. Surface Structure (Morphology)
sec.p: Surface morphological alterations in each biochar sample were examined at Adama Science and Technology University using a scanning electron microscope (JCM-6000Plus, JEOL Ltd., Tokyo, Japan).

sec.title: 2.7. Method of Data Analysis
sec.p: Microsoft Excel (Version 2108), OriginPro (Version 2025b), and ImageJ (Version 1.54t) were used for data processing and analysis. Excel was used to calculate kinetic parameters and process experimental data, OriginPro to generate and analyze TGA and DTG profiles, and ImageJ to measure biochar particle size from SEM micrographs. The physicochemical properties of the biochars were compared using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), followed by Tukey’s honestly significant difference (HSD) test at p < 0.05. Results are expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD) based on three independent biochar batches (n = 3). Different lowercase letters indicate significant differences among treatment means.

sec.title: 3.1. Effects of Heating Rate
sec.p: Figure 3 presents the TG profiles of corncob (CC), water hyacinth (WH), and their blends at heating rates of 5 and 20 °C/min. The heating rate had a limited effect on the overall pyrolysis pattern, although greater mass loss was generally observed at 5 °C/min [28]. The profiles can be broadly divided into three regions: moisture removal, major devolatilization, and gradual decomposition of the remaining thermally resistant fraction [29,30].

CC and WH contain cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, and extractive components, which contribute to differences in their thermal decomposition behavior [19]. Increasing the heating rate shifted the main DTG peak of CC from approximately 282.5 to 320.5 °C, while the maximum mass-loss rate increased from 67.5 to 72.6%/°C. This heating-rate effect is consistent with reported TGA studies of agricultural biomass [15,31]. Therefore, the results obtained at 5 °C/min were selected for subsequent thermal and kinetic analysis.

sec.title: 3.2. Thermal Decomposition Characteristics of Individual Feedstocks
sec.p: WH showed an earlier mass loss, with approximately 10.7% loss at 71.5 °C, mainly due to moisture evaporation as shown in Figure 4a. The main decomposition region was associated with the degradation of cellulose and hemicellulose [32]. Two major decomposition regions were observed, with peak temperatures of approximately 304 and 480.5 °C, followed by gradual decomposition of the remaining solid fraction up to 800 °C.

The TG and DTG profiles of CC showed three main decomposition regions as depicted in Figure 4b, reflecting the degradation of its different biomass components [33]. The initial region, from approximately 78.5 to 130 °C, was associated with moisture removal, while the major degradation region occurred between 196 and 460 °C and was mainly related to hemicellulose and cellulose decomposition. The maximum mass-loss rate was approximately 72.2%/°C. Variations in the shoulder and main peaks may be related to differences in biomass composition and structure [19,34].

sec.title: 3.3. Thermal Decomposition Behavior of the Blends
sec.p: Differences in cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin contents influence the thermal decomposition behavior of biomass feedstocks [35]. During co-pyrolysis, interactions among the components can further alter the decomposition characteristics of biomass blends [36]. At 5 °C/min, the onset and peak decomposition temperatures of the blends generally occurred between those of the individual CC and WH samples. At 20 °C/min, this pattern changed, indicating the influence of heating rate on the thermal decomposition behavior [37].

As shown in Table 5, the residual mass at 800 °C was lower for the blends than for WH but higher than for CC. At 5 °C/min, the residual mass increased in the order CC70:WH30 < CC50:WH50 < CC30:WH70. The maximum mass-loss rate also varied with blend composition and generally increased with increasing CC proportion, reflecting the effect of feedstock composition on thermal decomposition [36].
The TGA and DTG profiles of the three corncob–water hyacinth blends (CC50:WH50, CC70:WH30, and CC30:WH70) are presented in Figure 5.

sec.title: 3.4. Synergistic and Inhibitive Effects During Co-Pyrolysis
sec.p: The thermal interactions between CC and WH were assessed by comparing the experimental TG curves of the blends with their corresponding theoretical profiles calculated from the additive behavior of the individual feedstocks. Deviations between the experimental and theoretical curves indicate interactions among the components during co-pyrolysis [36].

For CC70:WH30, the experimental mass loss exceeded the theoretical value over part of the decomposition range as illustrated in Figure 6, indicating enhanced decomposition relative to the additive prediction. In contrast, CC50:WH50 and CC30:WH70 showed lower experimental mass loss than their theoretical profiles, suggesting inhibited decomposition and greater residual mass. These composition-dependent deviations demonstrate that the interaction between CC and WH varies with blend ratio [36]. However, the observed TG deviations represent thermal interaction effects and should not be interpreted solely as evidence of synergism without considering other kinetic and thermal parameters.

sec.title: 3.5. Reaction Mechanism Analysis Using the Master Plot Method
sec.p: The master plot analysis showed that the reaction behavior varied with conversion. At higher conversion levels (α = 0.8–0.9), the experimental data were generally closer to the power-law (P2) and nucleation-type models, as illustrated in Figure 7. At lower conversion levels, the D3 model, representing a three-dimensional diffusion-controlled mechanism, provided a better description of the reaction behavior [38].

After selecting the appropriate reaction model, the corresponding g(α) function was used in the Coats–Redfern analysis. A plot of ln[g(α)/T^2] against (1/T) was then used to estimate the kinetic parameters, as presented in Figure 8.

The apparent activation energies (Ea) of the blends differed from those of the individual feedstocks as indicated in Table 6, indicating changes in their apparent thermal decomposition kinetics [10]. The calculated pre-exponential factors (Ao) for the blends also varied with heating rate. At 5 °C/min, Ao ranged from 1.2057 × 105 to 1.45 × 1011 min−1, whereas at 20 °C/min it ranged from 5.987 × 103 to 1.31201 × 1011 min−1 at 20 °C/min. These variations reflect differences in the apparent kinetic characteristics of the blends and should be interpreted together with Ea and the corresponding reaction mechanism [39].

sec.title: 3.6. Results of Biochar Physicochemical Characterization
sec.p: Biochar yield ranged from 39.22% to 46.17%, with water hyacinth (WH) producing the lowest mean yield (39.22 ± 1.11%), corncob (CC) the highest (46.17 ± 0.60%), and the CC50 blend an intermediate yield (43.44 ± 0.42%). These differences may be associated with variations in feedstock composition, including lignin, cellulose, hemicellulose, and ash contents, which can influence solid-char formation during pyrolysis [40].

Bulk density differed significantly among the three biochar treatments (p < 0.05; Table 7). The CC50 blend had the highest bulk density (0.373 ± 0.015 g cm−3), followed by corncob (CC) biochar (0.310 ± 0.020 g cm−3) and water hyacinth (WH) biochar (0.240 ± 0.020 g cm−3). Tukey’s HSD test confirmed significant differences among all treatments. All biochars had bulk densities below 0.4 g cm−3, lower than the 0.47 g cm−3 reported by Kern et al. [41]. Biochar application has also been reported to reduce soil bulk density by 3–31%, depending on soil and biochar characteristics [42]. However, this effect was not directly assessed in the present study.

Pyrolysis substantially altered the proximate composition of both feedstocks. Volatile matter decreased from 75.23% to 20.22% for corncob and from 68.48% to 28.45% for water hyacinth, whereas fixed carbon increased from 13.74% to 43.11% and from 10.98% to 23.23%, respectively. Consequently, the VM/FC ratio decreased markedly, indicating greater carbon enrichment and improved biochar stability. The higher ash content may result from the concentration of inorganic constituents as volatile organic matter is removed during pyrolysis. These changes are consistent with the expected effects of pyrolysis and demonstrate effective devolatilization and formation of more carbon-rich biochars [43,44].

The proximate composition of the biochars is presented in Table 8. CC biochar had the highest fixed carbon (43.11%) and lowest VM/FC ratio (0.47), while WH biochar showed higher volatile matter (28.45%) and VM/FC ratio (1.22). The W50 blend exhibited intermediate values. The increase in ash content reflects the concentration of inorganic constituents following the loss of volatile matter during pyrolysis. The VM/FC ratio is commonly used as an indicator of biochar carbon stability, with values below 0.88 associated with longer estimated carbon persistence [45]. The relatively high ash content of WH biochar (44.12%) indicates a greater concentration of mineral constituents that may contribute to nutrient supply [46].

SEM images at 2000× magnification revealed distinct porous structures in the CC, WH, and blended biochars as seen in Figure 9. The blends exhibited more clearly developed pore structures than the individual feedstocks, suggesting greater structural development during co-pyrolysis. Similar porous structures have been reported for water-hyacinth biochar produced at 350 °C, with increasing pyrolysis temperature generally promoting pore development through greater removal of volatile components [4].

ImageJ analysis showed mean particle lengths of 3.346, 4.634, and 4.68 µm for WH, CC, and their blend, respectively, with corresponding mean areas of 0.154, 0.220, and 0.224 µm2 as summarized in Table 9. These micrometer-scale particles are relevant to soil–biochar interactions, as particle size can influence pore structure, water retention, and soil physical properties [47].

The biochar pH ranged from 9.34 to 9.56, indicating alkaline characteristics. However, pH did not differ significantly among the three treatments (p > 0.05). The alkaline nature of biochar suggests potential for ameliorating acidic soils, although its effect depends on the initial soil pH, biochar properties, and application rate [46].

Electrical conductivity (EC) differed significantly among the three biochars. WH biochar had the highest EC (23.92 ± 0.69 mS cm−1), followed by the CC50 blend (8.67 ± 0.87 mS cm−1) and CC biochar (6.78 ± 0.37 mS cm−1). The high EC of WH biochar suggests a greater concentration of soluble ions, which may increase salinity risk depending on the application rate and receiving soil properties [48].

Cation exchange capacity (CEC) differed significantly among the three biochars. The CC50:WH50 blend had the highest CEC (35.06 ± 0.55 cmol kg−1), followed by WH biochar (26.24 ± 0.54 cmol kg−1) and CC biochar (13.88 ± 0.31 cmol kg−1). The higher CEC of the blend suggests greater potential for retaining exchangeable cations, although this capacity depends on biochar surface properties and feedstock composition [49].

Total nitrogen (TN) and available phosphorus (P) differed significantly among the three biochar treatments (p < 0.05). WH biochar had the highest TN content (1.500 ± 0.030%), followed by the CC50 blend (1.317 ± 0.087%) and CC biochar (0.573 ± 0.045%). A similar trend was observed for available P, with WH biochar showing the highest concentration (538.763 ± 1.591 mg kg−1), followed by the CC50 blend (454.393 ± 2.313 mg kg−1) and CC biochar (418.817 ± 2.407 mg kg−1). These differences suggest that feedstock selection and blending influence the nutrient composition of the resulting biochar. Previous studies have also reported that the nutrient characteristics of biochar vary with feedstock type and pyrolysis conditions [4,50].

sec.title: 4. Conclusions
sec.p: This study investigated the thermal decomposition, kinetic behavior, and physicochemical properties of biochars produced from corncob (CC), water hyacinth (WH), and their blend (CC50:WH50). Coats–Redfern analysis yielded apparent activation energies of 135.4, 73.23, and 96.4 kJ mol−1 for CC, WH, and CC50, respectively, indicating a deviation from additive behavior that does not, by itself, confirm synergism. At 350 °C, the mean biochar yields were 46.17%, 39.22%, and 43.44%, respectively, with significant differences among treatments. All biochars were alkaline (pH 9.34–9.56), with no significant difference in pH. However, electrical conductivity, total nitrogen, available phosphorus, cation exchange capacity, and bulk density differed significantly among treatments. WH biochar had the highest electrical conductivity, total nitrogen, and available phosphorus, while CC50:WH50 had the highest cation exchange capacity and bulk density. These findings demonstrate that feedstock selection and blending influence biochar yield and physicochemical properties. Further soil-incubation and plant-growth studies are required to determine the suitability of these biochars for agricultural application, particularly considering the high electrical conductivity of WH biochar.
